prompt: Relational algebra can be built from a minimal set of six operators, with the rest defined in terms of them. Which of these belong to that minimal set? Select all that apply.

options.explanation: Correct. Product is primitive; every join is defined as a product followed by a selection.
Correct. Difference is primitive, and intersection is derived from it: the intersection of R and S is R minus the part of R that is not in S.
Derived: it is a product, a selection on equal shared attributes, and a projection to drop the duplicate columns.
Derived from difference: R minus (R minus S). A common mistake is to assume all three set operators are primitive.
Correct. Rename is needed so that, for example, a relation can be combined with a copy of itself.

workedExample:
The six primitives are selection σ, projection π, rename ρ, union ∪, difference − and Cartesian product ×. Everything else is shorthand:

```formula
R ⋈θ S = σθ (R × S)
R ∩ S = R − (R − S)
where
R, S: relations with disjoint headings for the theta-join line and union-compatible headings for the intersection line
⋈θ: theta join: combine relational tuples satisfying the condition θ (theta)
⋈: natural join (no condition): match on all shared attribute names
σθ: selection σ (the Greek letter sigma) with condition θ: keep relational tuples where θ is true
π: projection (pi): keep only the listed attributes
ρ: rename (rho): give a relation or attribute a new name
×: Cartesian product: every relational tuple of R paired with every relational tuple of S
∪: union: relational tuples in either input
∩: intersection: relational tuples in both
−: difference: relational tuples in R but not in S
÷: division: values paired with every relational tuple of S
In words: a join is a product then a selection; intersection is R minus the part of R not in S. Division (÷) is also built from π, × and −.
```

Check the intersection rule on numbers:

```formula
R = {1, 2, 3} and S = {2, 3, 4}
R − S = {1}
R − (R − S) = {2, 3} = R ∩ S
where
R, S: two small example sets
{ }: a set of distinct values
−: difference
∩: intersection
In words: removing from R the part not in S leaves exactly what R and S share.
```

prompt:
Local fixture (course titles are omitted):

```
Student        Enrolled   Course
sid name year  sid cid    cid dept
 1  Ada   2     1  DB     DB  CS
 2  Ben   1     1  OS     OS  CS
 3  Cat   2     1  LA     LA  MA
 4  Dev   3     2  DB
                3  DB
                3  OS
```

Student has four rows, Enrolled six and Course three. Dev has no enrolment. The attributes are student id `sid`, student `name`, study `year`, course code `cid`, and department `dept`.

Which expression returns the sids of students enrolled on course labelled OS but **not** on LA? The options use this notation:

```formula
π sid (σ cid='OS' (Enrolled))
where
π: projection: keep only the listed attribute, removing duplicates
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition after it is true
sid, cid: the student-id and course-code attributes
Enrolled: the enrolment relation (sid, cid)
In words: the ids of the students on course labelled OS. The options combine expressions like this with − (difference: in the left, not the right), ∩ (intersection: in both), ∧ (and) and ≠ (not equal).
```

options.text:
```formula
π sid (σ cid='OS' ∧ cid≠'LA'
(Enrolled))
where
Enrolled: the local relation of student id sid and course code cid
sid: student identifier
cid: course code; quoted text is a literal code
σ: selection: retain relational tuples satisfying the next condition
π: projection: retain the listed attributes, removing duplicates
∧: and: both conditions must hold
≠: not equal
In words: Keep enrolments on the course labelled OS whose own course code differs from LA, then list student ids. This tests one relational tuple at a time.
```
options.explanation: The condition is tested per relational tuple. Every course labelled OS relational tuple has cid ≠ 'LA', so this returns everyone on course labelled OS, including Ada, who also takes LA.

options.text:
```formula
π sid (σ cid='OS' (Enrolled)) − π sid
(σ cid='LA' (Enrolled))
where
Enrolled: the local relation of student id sid and course code cid
sid: student identifier
cid: course code; quoted text is a literal code
σ: selection: retain relational tuples satisfying the next condition
π: projection: retain the listed attributes, removing duplicates
−: difference: retain left relational tuples absent from the right
In words: List students on the course labelled OS, then remove students on LA.
```
options.explanation: Correct. {1, 3} − {1} = {3}. 'Not on LA' is a property of the student across relational tuples, which needs set difference, not a row filter.

options.text:
```formula
π sid (σ cid='OS' (Enrolled)) ∩ π sid
(σ cid='LA' (Enrolled))
where
Enrolled: the local relation of student id sid and course code cid
sid: student identifier
cid: course code; quoted text is a literal code
σ: selection: retain relational tuples satisfying the next condition
π: projection: retain the listed attributes, removing duplicates
∩: intersection: retain relational tuples common to both sides
In words: List students on both the course labelled OS and LA.
```
options.explanation: Intersection gives students on both courses: {1}, the opposite of what is asked.

options.text:
```formula
π sid (σ cid='LA' (Enrolled)) − π sid
(σ cid='OS' (Enrolled))
where
Enrolled: the local relation of student id sid and course code cid
sid: student identifier
cid: course code; quoted text is a literal code
σ: selection: retain relational tuples satisfying the next condition
π: projection: retain the listed attributes, removing duplicates
−: difference: retain left relational tuples absent from the right
In words: List students on LA, then remove students on the course labelled OS.
```
options.explanation: Operands reversed: this gives students on LA but not course labelled OS, which is {1} − {1, 3} = ∅.

workedExample:
```formula
π sid (σ cid='OS' (Enrolled)) = {1, 3}
π sid (σ cid='LA' (Enrolled)) = {1}
{1, 3} − {1} = {3}
where
π: projection: keep only the listed attribute, removing duplicates
σ: selection: keep relational tuples where the condition is true; quoted values are literal course codes
sid, cid: the student-id and course-code attributes
Enrolled: the enrolment relation
{ }: a set of distinct values
−: difference: values on the left that are not on the right
In words: students 1 and 3 take course labelled OS, student 1 takes LA, so only student 3 (Cat) takes course labelled OS but not LA.
```

Why option A fails: σ looks at one relational tuple at a time. Ada's (1, course labelled OS) relational tuple passes the test "cid is course labelled OS and cid is not LA", so Ada wrongly appears. "Not in some other relational tuple" needs − (or `NOT EXISTS` in SQL).
